claims.claim: laboratory, 2.5 °C, 150 d: 68.4–71.2 % of white perch died; yellow perch 0.8 % (Johnson & Evans 1990, 1991, abstracts)
claims.note: the 1991 abstract gives 71.2 % (white perch) and 0.8 % (yellow perch) after 150 d at 2.5 °C; 68.4 % is not in it (presumably from the 1990 paper)

claims.claim: laboratory, 4.0 °C, starved 180 d: 40.6 % died (none when fed); mortality highest in the smallest
claims.note: credited to Johnson & Evans 1990, not this entry; nothing of it is in the 1991 abstract

claims.claim: after 150 days at 2.5 °C, 71.2 % of white perch died against 0.8 % of yellow perch; at 4.0 °C 11.1 % against 17.7 %
claims.note: the abstract gives these four figures

claims.claim: white perch "remained active throughout the winter" while yellow perch rested on the bottom and used 25.8 % less oxygen (at 4 °C)
claims.note: the abstract has the quoted words (laboratory tanks) and 'consumed 25.8% less oxygen than white perch' during the inactive wintering period at 4.0 °C

claims.claim: similar-sized white perch died at 3.3 times the yellow perch rate in Great Lakes-type winters; their young die 3.3× faster than yellow perch's over a first winter
claims.note: in the abstract this is a model prediction, not an observation: multiple regressions of overwinter mortality on fall length and winter duration 'predict 3.3 times greater mortality' for white perch than similar-sized yellow perch at Great Lakes winter regimes. '3.3 times greater mortality' is not the same as '3.3× faster' (a rate); the full text is needed to know which

claims.claim: field young perch stop growing below ~10–13.5 °C and live on their autumn lipid, so first-winter mortality is size-selective (Post & Evans 1989; Johnson & Evans 1990, 1991)
claims.note: the abstract says only that in the laboratory 'small fish died first' in both species; no growth threshold is in it

claims.claim: white perch's higher routine metabolism costs them more over winter than yellow perch
claims.note: the abstract: yellow perch had a lower routine metabolic rate and consumed body energy more gradually; at 2.5 °C they lost 24.6 % less dry weight than similar-sized white perch
